title: Amsterdam and London: A Tale of Two Cities

content_html_sanitized:
This is Richard Cowan with the 420 Marijuana Headline News.

It’s 420. Do you know where your freedom is? https://youtu.be/08BijaBNro8?si=euPhnKUwvE4VZ5tQ

With apologies to Charles Dickens, I need to borrow the opening line from his most famous novel, but in the present tense: It is the best of times. It is the worst of times. 


Yesterday, the London Drug Commission, authorized by the Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, published its report, recommending that the possession of small amounts of cannabis be decriminalized. 


Essentially, the justification for this revolutionary, extraordinary, radical, unprecedented, unheard of, unbelievable, expealidocious recommendation, is that arresting mostly young black men, aggravates racial tensions and wastes police resources. Thank goodness, that never happened in America.


Actually, “Black Americans are arrested for violating marijuana possession laws at nearly four times the rates of white Americans, yet both consume marijuana at roughly the same rates.

See  Racial Disparity in Marijuana Arrests


Frankly, I am not optimistic about any changes in the UK., because in 2000, I reported The Complete Intellectual and Moral Bankruptcy of UK Cannabis Policies. 3 Articles. But sometimes they faked me out.


The Labor government has already made clear that it will not act on the Commission’s advice. So, I will believe it when I see it.


In the meantime, the reason that I referred to Amsterdam in the title is that the report has a section on the Dutch cannabis policy, which is excellent, as far as it goes. But it stopped just as it was getting to the important point, that de facto legalization of retail sales of cannabis actually works and did not destroy the country. 


Of course, in fairness to the Commission, it’s only been working for a little over forty nine years. (By the way, not just in Amsterdam, but in almost every town in the country.)


Of course, this omission is hardly unique, and of all the absurdities of cannabis prohibition, nothing puzzles me more than the invisibility of The Netherlands. It is not some exotic land, far, far away. To make matters even weirder, consider this from 1999.

Two Stories About Holland: UK Police Are Taking British 16-Yearolds To Visit Dutch "Cannabis Cafes" As A Part Of Drug Education; And A Dutch City Is "subsidising work experience for the unemployed in coffee shops selling marijuana."  -- Common Sense -- But Not Without Controversy.


Although Amsterdam is famous for its Red Light District and - of course- its coffee shops- that also sell coffee, the country ranks well below very Prohibitionist countries like France in per capita cannabis consumption. See Prevalence of cannabis use in the last year in Europe as of 2022, by country


Moreover, The Netherlands always ranks in the top ten of countries that are best for raising families.

See Europe: Quality of Life Index by Country 2024


Note that on this list, The Netherlands ranks second, while the United Kingdom ranks eighteenth. 


Now, in fairness to the Commission, and to the UK generally, they are hardly alone in being unable to find The Netherlands. 


Germany, which has a long border with The Netherlands, and where they recently legalized possession and private cultivation, seemed to have misplaced their maps, and acted like they were doing something that had never been done before. 

See Germany's first year of legalized cannabis: Has it worked?


Meanwhile in Belgium, which is on The Netherlands’ southern border, adults over the age of 18 are allowed to possess up to 3 grams. Perhaps the UK should just go Belgian. 


Obviously, Mayor Khan understands the difficulties in getting anything done and so he had to settle for the minimum. One would assume that he and the Commission Chairman, Lord Falconer

planned accordingly. 


Ironically, Lord Falconer is originally from Edinburgh, Scotland, which actually has one of the worst hard drug problems and the highest rate of teen cannabis use in Europe.

See Scotland Forever? Not With This Drugs Policy!


But to make matters even more bizarre, this story is from 1998:

Meanwhile In Scotland, Senior Scottish Law Lord Calls for Royal Commission To Study "Legalization" of Cannabis – The Independent 

And More Calls for Legalizing Cannabis Come from Influential Sources In Scotland and London. -- 2 Articles


Because of stories like this, I was sometimes optimistic twenty years ago about cannabis reform in the UK, but not now. 

I say that the best two word explanation for cannabis prohibition in the United States is “bad journalism”, but in the UK I would need to exhaust a Thesaurus even to begin to describe how utterly wretched the coverage is. I will be following up on this story next week, but don’t hold your breath, unless you’re vaping.
